evidence.claim: Marion’s Main Street burned on a Sunday morning in November 1894. Fire began behind the courthouse in a building called the Ark, then spread through a downtown built largely of wood.
evidence.quote: Until the late 19th century, Main Street was a collection of mostly wooden huts, houses, and buildings. On Sunday morning, November 25, 1894 a fire sprang up in an old building known as the "Ark" located behind the Courthouse.

evidence.claim: Even the few brick buildings were gutted. With no public water supply, residents formed bucket brigades, but most of the street was destroyed.
evidence.quote: The few brick buildings on Main Street were also gutted, and because there was no public water supply, bucket brigades were hurriedly formed to halt the advance of the fire. It was not enough, however, and most of Main Street was burned to the ground.

evidence.claim: Botanist Bill Moye documented many of its rare and endangered plants, and his work helped expand the park. Much of the park remains undeveloped wilderness, within a heavily forested mountain range.
evidence.quote: The park, like most of the South Mountains, is largely undeveloped, and much of it is still wilderness. Numerous rare and endangered plants lie within its boundaries, much of them documented by botanist Bill Moye, whose efforts helped expand the park to its present size.

evidence.claim: Near town, the John Lattimore House records an earlier pattern of building. A one-room log structure from the early 19th century gained a frame addition, a full-length porch and rear shed rooms in the 1820s or 1830s. The house rests on fieldstone piers beneath a gable roof.
evidence.quote: It is a vernacular one-story-with-raised-attic dwelling consisting of a one-room, half-dovetailed log structure dated to the early 19th century, with a frame addition, full-length porch, and rear shed rooms added in the 1820s or 1830s.  It has a gable roof and sits on a fieldstone pier foundation.

flags: Partial overview: all three guidebook cache files have identical bodies ending at printed page 51, before South Mountain Scenery. Only the contents entry supports designation; the specific scenic rationale, route limits, drive time and road-building history are unavailable. Overview is shorter than requested rather than padding that gap.

Dropped unsupported current claims: 34-mile byway, Metcalf/Shelby starting point, roadside cornfields and apple orchards, Polkville in the First Broad River valley, Cherry Mountain and cherry bounce, and Cherokee name Oakanoahs. Orchard motif removed because the new story has no supported orchard content.
Order reversed from current to match material’s Marion-first strip. Park remains a separate excursion; cache does not establish a direct byway entrance or present access status.
Marion sources disagree on courthouse construction date and number of district buildings; neither disputed detail is used.
South Mountains source gives ambiguous Cherokee or Catawba attribution without a community source. That history is omitted rather than assigning it to one nation.
